units.translation: And my father sends help from the tomb.
Why ever do you not approach for help?
[I filled out the defective verse by adding the words
if these things seem helpful to you.
I call upon the queen of this land, Athena, to come as my helper.
But you, testimonies and proofs, are called helpers of justice and oaths.
of whom the helpers are already beneath the earth
But I will come bringing helpers and advocates.
Come as a helper to the city.

Hence Nauck thinks that what Photius has at p. 497, 14 is repeated: σάλα: φροντίς [care, anxiety]. οὕτως Αἰσχύλος [thus Aeschylus]: which, with the name of Aeschylus omitted, Suidas explains by φροντίς [care, anxiety], Hesychius by φροντίς [care, anxiety] and βλάβη [harm]. A word of similar form is uáva, about which Photius p. 246, 4.
ἀσαλής [unshaken]: she who is without care, who takes thought for nothing. For σάλη [care] is anxiety. ἀσαλής [unshaken] is the one without worry.
ἀσαλής μανία [unshaken madness]: she who takes thought for nothing; for σάλη [care] is anxiety. Thus Aeschylus.
σάλα: φροντίς [care, anxiety]. οὕτως Αἰσχύλος [thus Aeschylus]
not to be soothed by flattery
who cannot be soothed by flattery (σαίνεσθαι [to be fawned upon]).
The spirit from my mother is not to be soothed.
It is said properly of fire. Improperly of the waves of the sea that never cease
Hesychius explains it by ἀκατάπαυστος [unceasing]. Similarly Aeschylus uses the verb κατασβεννύναι [to quench] at Ag. 958
the unquenchable passage from father Ocean.
There is the sea; who will quench it?
For other examples see Thes. vol. 1, 2 p. 2151.
acting impiously toward a god or some stranger.
they perished by an impious thought.
breathing out his life by an impious death.
the impious marriage of the sons of Aegyptus.
and taking their obscure things immediately in ignorance.
Art is far weaker than necessity.
Is Zeus then weaker than these?
he remains not panting at all.
like a horse panting at the bit he remains.
where Meineke reads Ασιανάν [Asian] for Ασίαν δήν [Asian land], examples of which form are found in Thucydides and others, as indicated in Thes. vol. 1, 2 p. 2166, but none among the tragedians.
the warlike lord of populous Asia.
throughout the Asian land they are no longer ruled by Persians,
the boundary of Asia, the Phasis.
Elmsley reads Ἀσίδα [Asian] and Ασίδος [of Asian], with the first syllable lengthened, which is read
where he imitates a verse of Archilochus
